cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), Yiwu seed-grown gardens, many regrown from old trees pruned low in the 1980s
processing: Classic Yiwu raw pu-erh: pan-fired, lightly hand-rolled, sun-dried and loosely stone-pressed, keeping the long leaf whole.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the reference harvest; autumn Mahei is common and gentle.
appearance_dry: Long, loosely twisted dark-green leaves with silver buds and long stems, in a loose easily pried cake.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold, bright and clear, turning amber with age.
appearance_wet: Long, supple, yellow-green leaves on long stems, the textbook Yiwu look.
taste_profile: The textbook Yiwu cup: honey, orchid and a soft fruitiness, low bitterness, a smooth oily body and a sweetness that rises slowly in the throat and stays.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Porcelain, short early steeps and patience; the throat sweetness shows up after the third or fourth infusion, not in the first.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and tree class (gushu, da shu, 'small tree' from the regrown and newer gardens), as cakes and maocha from many boutique producers, and it has been a named origin longer than most Yiwu villages, so mid-aged Mahei (roughly 2006–2016) is genuinely available. Young (1–3 years) it is floral and light; it is at its best between about 7 and 15 years, when the honey thickens into dried fruit; pre-2005 Mahei exists mostly as unlabelled Yiwu cakes. Supply is 2005–2025, with Kunming-dry examples staying bright and Guangdong-stored ones turning darker and sweeter sooner.
description:
Mahei is the village that defines what people mean by 'Yiwu flavour': a settlement a few kilometres from Yiwu town, at around 1,200–1,300 m, whose gardens (together with neighbouring hamlets such as Luoshuidong) produced the reference cakes of the Yiwu revival. If a vendor wants to show a newcomer classic Yiwu, Mahei is usually what they pour.

The gardens are seed-grown trees, and here lies an important detail: in the 1980s many of Mahei's old trees were pruned down to bush height to make picking easier, and they have since regrown into sizeable trees. So 'old tree' Mahei is genuinely old at the root but not the towering forest tree a wrapper might suggest. Processing is textbook Yiwu: light firing, gentle rolling, sun drying and a loose press that keeps the leaves long.

In the cup Mahei is honey, orchid and soft fruit, with low bitterness, a smooth oily body and a returning sweetness that climbs in the throat from the third steep onwards. It is less wild and intense than the state-forest teas and less sugary than Bingdao, which makes it steady, reliable and very easy to drink young or mid-aged. Keep the early steeps short and let it build.

Sold by spring year and tree class, from many producers, and because the village is sizeable and well known, supply is better and prices are saner than for Guafengzhai or Bohetang. The common dodge is lower-slope or terrace tea sold as Mahei gushu; it will still taste of Yiwu, just thinner and shorter.

Buy one Mahei cake to drink now and one to leave for ten years; it is the classic Yiwu to learn ageing on.
sources_note: The 1980s low-pruning of Mahei's old gardens is widely reported by producers and vendors who work there; the exact extent varies by garden.
